lead.headline: Every clue is true.
lead.dek:
Project Scroll now has a new, free online treasure hunt.
Real mysteries, history and clues hide in pages, websites,
county histories, survey maps, certificates, newspapers,
forgotten lore and local legends.
Every one of them can be solved by you.

stories.headline: A lodge of E Clampus Vitus, in Cassopolis, in 1846
stories.dek: Two county histories record a lodge of the “Ancient and Honorable Order of the Eclampsus Vitus” at Cassopolis in the spring of 1846, with its charter members named and a ball of two hundred badges.
pic: /img/news/e-clampus-vitus-in-cassopolis-1846
Howard S. Rogers, History of Cass County, from 1825 to 1875, page 253: the first secret society of which there is any record
Rogers, History of Cass County, from 1825 to 1875 (1875), p. 253.
body: Cassopolis, Mich. “The first Secret Society, of which there is any record, was a Lodge of the ‘Ancient and Honorable Order of the Eclampsus Vitus,’ which was instituted in the spring of 1846, with Dr. E. J. Bonine, Laban Harter, J. P. Osborn and Dr. L. Osborn as charter members.” So wrote Howard S. Rogers in his History of Cass County, from 1825 to 1875, published in 1875, on page 253.

It was, he says, a lodge “in broadest burlesque of legitimate secret organizations.” Candidates were bound fast, blindfolded and dragged into the hall by halters, and made to pledge themselves to things impossible or ridiculous. In the winter of 1846 and 1847 the lodge gave a grand ball at the Union Hotel, where more than two hundred of its badges were displayed, “by men who stood among the highest in popular esteem and respectability.”
Alfred Mathews told the story again in his History of Cass County, Michigan in 1882, on page 174. Both books say the order was afterward merged into the “Sons of Malta.”

Why it matters: E Clampus Vitus is known today as the historical society of the old West, the “Clampers” who put up plaques across California. The order dates its founding to 1845, at Lewisport, Virginia, now West Union, West Virginia, and a lodge was organized at Mokelumne Hill, California, in 1851. If the Cass County histories are right, a lodge was meeting in a small Michigan county seat in 1846, within a year of that founding date.
Did the Cassopolis lodge ever have a real charter, or only a joke one? That is Case 1 on the board, and nobody has cracked it yet. Both books are free to read online.
sources: Howard S. Rogers, History of Cass County, from 1825 to 1875 (1875), pp. 253–254, University of Michigan
Alfred Mathews, History of Cass County, Michigan (1882), p. 174, University of Michigan

stories.headline: The day 3,000 people came to watch one log
stories.short: The day 3,000 came to watch one log
stories.dek: Twenty-four men carried the first log of the Pioneer Log Cabin while a band played. Four weeks later the cabin was finished.
body: Cassopolis, Mich. At half past eight on the morning of 23 May 1923, a black walnut log twenty-six feet long was carried to its place by twenty-four men. A band played and the crowd sang. About three thousand people stood and watched, and many had driven up to fifty miles to be there.
It was the first log of the Cass County Pioneer Log Cabin. A note written on the back of one card of the day says fifty-two volunteers did the first morning’s work.

The logs came from families across the county, given from their own land. Each log was numbered, and a list kept the family’s name, the town and the kind of tree. The card printed for the occasion gives the whole job in one line: May 23 to June 20, 1923. Four weeks, from the first log to Pioneer Day.
The cabin still stands in Cassopolis today, as the Pioneer Log Cabin Museum.
cta: See the cards of the day
The museum, its hours and directions
sources: Laying first log of Cass County Pioneer Cabin, Cassopolis, Michigan (postcard, 1923), Burton Historical Collection, Detroit Public Library
Men building the Cass County Pioneer Cabin, Cassopolis, Michigan (postcard, 1923), Burton Historical Collection, Detroit Public Library

stories.headline: Pick a date, and see what’s open
stories.short: Pick a date, and see what’s open
stories.dek: Tell the Visit & Plan page the day you’re coming. It shows the museums open that day, what’s on, and your own day on the map.
body: The St. Joseph River valley. Many of the valley’s museums are run by volunteers and open only a few days a week, some only in summer. Turning up to a locked door is the commonest way a day out goes wrong.
The Visit & Plan page now takes a date. Pick the day you’re coming and it shows which museums are open, using each place’s posted hours, and any festival on that day.
There are ready-made days out to start from, each one in an order that saves driving and opens in Google Maps with one tap. Or build your own day, and see it on the map with rough times.
Hours change, and the page can’t know about holidays, so check each place before you go.

stories.headline: Send someone an old postcard
stories.dek: Pick any card in the gallery, write on the back, and share it from your phone.
body: Cassopolis, Mich. A century ago this is how you told someone you were thinking of them: a picture of your town on the front, a few lines on the back, and a stamp.
Every card in the old postcard gallery now has a button under it: Send this postcard. Write who it’s to, your message and your name, and the back of the card is laid out as you type.
Then share it straight from your phone, or save the picture to post, text or print.
Nothing you write is sent to Project Scroll. The card is made on your own phone or computer.
pic: /img/news/send-someone-an-old-postcard
Road to Town, Cassopolis, Mich., on an old real-photo postcard
Road to Town, Cassopolis, Mich., about 1908 to 1915. Private collection.

stories.headline: Did the joke lodge of 1846 ever have a real charter?
stories.short: Case 1: did the lodge of 1846 have a charter?
stories.dek: Nobody has cracked Case 1 yet. The book that first told the story is free to read online, and the clue is one word.
body: Cassopolis, Mich. In the spring of 1846, the county histories say, a lodge of the “Ancient and Honorable Order of the Eclampsus Vitus” was founded at Cassopolis, all halters and blindfolds. That winter it gave a grand ball at the Union Hotel, where more than two hundred of its badges were on show.
Howard S. Rogers told the story first, in his History of Cass County, from 1825 to 1875 (1875), on pages 253 and 254. He names four charter members. Alfred Mathews printed the story again in 1882.
So the question on the case board is simple to ask and hard to settle: was there ever a real charter, or only a joke one? Read the two books side by side, and watch the word “charter.”
The first person to answer it, with the book and the page, is named on the case board for good.
pic: /img/news/case-1-is-still-open
Alfred Mathews, History of Cass County, Michigan (1882), page 174: the lodge of the Eclampsus Vitus
Mathews, History of Cass County, Michigan (1882), p. 174, where the story is told again.

stories.headline: A depot, a water tower and three clues
stories.short: A depot, a water tower, three clues
stories.dek: An old real-photo postcard of a station somewhere in the valley. Can you name the town?
body: A small wooden depot. A water tower on iron legs. A field of tall grass, and not one person in sight. The card’s caption has been cut off, and the station sign blurred.
Clue one. The railroad here was the Michigan Central’s Air Line, which ran from Jackson to Niles.
Clue two. The town is in Cass County, east of Cassopolis.
Clue three. The Air Line came through in 1871, and the station was set up the same year.
stories.reveal: Vandalia. The caption at the foot of the card reads “R.R. Station Vandalia Mich.” The town’s other cards show the same depot with a train at the platform, and with passengers and a baggage cart. The Air Line between Jackson and Niles was abandoned in 1937.
pic: /img/news/where-is-this
A small wooden depot and a water tower on iron legs, on an old real-photo postcard; the station sign is blurred

stories.headline: The hotel that walked away
stories.dek: In 1867 the old hotel where the lodge held its ball was hauled across Cassopolis and turned into a mill. Where did it end up?
pic: /img/news/the-hotel-that-walked
The hotel’s block on the 1860 wall map of Cass County, Van Buren and Berrien counties
The hotel’s block on the 1860 Geil, Harley & Siverd wall map. Library of Congress.
body: Cassopolis, Mich. The old hotel stood at the northwest corner of Broadway and State Street, at the heart of the village.

It was the Union Hotel, where the lodge of 1846 held its grand ball. In 1852 the Masons held their first meeting under the same roof, and on the 1860 wall map of the county the engraver cut one word on its block: HOTEL.
Then, in 1867, the building was hauled across the village and turned into a mill, and a new hotel rose on its ground.
Where did the old hotel end up, and is any of it still standing? That is Case 2 on the board. The first sources are the county histories of 1882 and 1906, free to read online.
cta: Drag the corner from 1860 to today

stories.headline: Fly over Cassopolis, laser point by laser point
stories.dek: 355,650 real laser points from the 2015 survey, in 3D, with the 1860 town plan laid on the ground.
body: Cassopolis, Mich. In 2015 an aircraft flew over Cass County firing laser pulses at the ground, hundreds of thousands a second, and timing each echo. Every dot in the new model is one of those echoes, from the blocks around the courthouse: 355,650 of them.
The buildings and trees stand where the laser found them, 125,189 points of roofs and 230,461 of trees, over the bare ground of the town.
Press “1860 plan” and the old town plan from the county wall map is laid on the ground beneath them. Raise the heights, tilt it, fly around it, or go full screen.
Fly over it, and you earn the Laser surveyor badge.
pic: /img/news/cassopolis-in-lidar
Cassopolis in 3D: buildings in gold and trees in green, drawn from 355,650 laser points of the 2015 survey
Cassopolis in LiDAR: every dot is one laser echo from the 2015 survey.

stories.headline: Stoves, lures, wagons and guitars
stories.dek: Twenty-three makers from the valley: what they made, how they ended, and where you can still see their work.
body: The St. Joseph River valley. For a century the towns of the valley made things the whole country knew by name.

Round Oak stoves came out of Dowagiac from 1871. James Heddon’s Sons made fishing lures there from 1902. Studebaker built wagons in South Bend, then cars. Gibson made mandolins and guitars in Kalamazoo, and C. G. Conn made band instruments in Elkhart.
The new Made in the Valley page follows twenty-three of them: who founded each one, what it made, when it peaked, how it ended, and the museums where its work is still on show.
Every maker is pinned on a map, and set on a timeline that runs from the 1850s to today.
cta: The makers on a map and a timeline

stories.headline: Company D: the 85 men Dowagiac sent in 1861
stories.dek: Raised at Dowagiac in the summer of 1861: who they were, where they fought, and the nineteen who did not come home.
pic: /img/news/company-d-sixth-michigan
Monument Day, Dowagiac, Mich.: a great crowd around a monument, on a real-photo postcard
Monument Day, Dowagiac, on a real-photo postcard. Tinder Collection, Clements Library, University of Michigan.
body: Dowagiac, Mich. In the summer of 1861 a company was raised at Dowagiac, the second organized in Cass County, under Captain Charles E. Clarke. It became Company D of the Sixth Michigan Infantry.

The regiment gathered at Kalamazoo and left for the East on 30 August 1861, 944 strong. After garrison duty at Baltimore it went to New Orleans and the lower Mississippi, fought at Baton Rouge, and joined the assault on Port Hudson on 27 May 1863, where Lieutenant Frederick J. Clarke was killed. It ended the war as heavy artillery, and was discharged at Jackson, Michigan, on 5 September 1865.
Of its men, four were killed or died of wounds and fifteen died of disease. As in the whole war, sickness killed more of them than battle did.
The roll of all 85 men, as Mathews printed it in 1882, is now on the site, checked line by line against the page scans, with this week’s anniversaries from their service.
sources: Alfred Mathews, History of Cass County, Michigan (1882), pp. 117–120, University of Michigan

stories.headline: Who was in town in 1860?
stories.dek: 331 names from the business directories printed beside the old town plans, with the men of Company D, in one roll you can search.
pic: /img/news/who-was-in-town-in-1860
The Cassopolis business directory beside the village plan on the 1860 wall map: hotels, merchants, physicians and surgeons
The Cassopolis directory beside the village plan, 1860 wall map. Library of Congress.
body: The St. Joseph River valley. Beside each town plan on the old county maps, the mapmakers printed a business directory: the lawyers, doctors, merchants, smiths, hotel keepers and county officers who paid to be listed.
Now 331 of those entries, from Cassopolis, Dowagiac, Niles and Paw Paw in 1860 and Goshen in 1861, are in one roll you can search by surname, trade or town, together with the 85 men of Company D.

A directory is not a census. It lists the people who paid to appear, so most farmers, labourers, women and children are not in it. But a directory line puts a person in a town, in a trade, in a year, and that is often the first step to finding a family.
Every entry links to its map, so you can find the name in the engraving yourself.

stories.headline: Eleven more old postcards
stories.dek: The Pioneer Log Cabin going up in 1923, the depots at Cassopolis and Vandalia, Chicago Street in Edwardsburg, Main Street in Niles and a steam shovel at White Pigeon.
pic: /img/news/eleven-more-old-postcards
Main Street, now Broadway, Cassopolis: a long arched brick block with awnings, on an early postcard
Main Street, now Broadway, Cassopolis, about 1905 to 1912. Private collection.
body: Cassopolis, Mich. Eleven more cards have joined the old postcard gallery, all from before 1931 and so in the public domain.

Two show the Pioneer Log Cabin going up in May and June of 1923. There are the Michigan Central depots at Cassopolis and Vandalia, the corner of State and Main in Vandalia, the north side of Chicago Street in Edwardsburg, a crowd on Main Street in Niles, and the long arched block on what was then Main Street, now Broadway, in Cassopolis.
White Pigeon joins the gallery for the first time, with a steam shovel at work on the paper mill track.
Every card can be searched, found on the map, and sent as a postcard of your own.

stories.headline: The harvest trail: a mill, an orchard and the stove town
stories.dek: Stamp three places in your passport this fall, from September to November, and earn the harvest badge.
pic: /img/news/the-harvest-trail
An orchard at its best, near Benton Harbor and St. Joseph, Mich., on a linen postcard
An orchard at its best, near Benton Harbor and St. Joseph, about 1930 to 1945. Boston Public Library, Tichnor Brothers Collection.
body: The St. Joseph River valley. Fall is harvest time in the valley, and the passport has a trail just for it.
The mill. Bonneyville Mill near Bristol, Indiana, a county park around a historic grist mill that still grinds flour, open Tuesday to Sunday until mid-November.
The orchard. Jollay Orchards near Coloma, where the same family has farmed since 1857: u-pick fruit, fresh cider and apple-cinnamon doughnuts.
The stove town. The Dowagiac Area History Museum, free, where the story of the Round Oak Stove Company is told.
Press “I’m here” at all three between September and November of the same year, and the harvest badge is yours. Check each place’s hours before you go.

stories.headline: A paper passport to stamp, and a teachers’ pack
stories.dek: A passport booklet with a stamp box for every place, a one-day field trip for classes, and the valley kitchen as a little book.
body: The St. Joseph River valley. The passport on Project Scroll lives in your phone: press “I’m here” at a museum, a walk stop, a table or a festival, and the stamp lands in it.
Now there is a paper one too. Print the booklet, fold it, and carry it. Every place in the valley has its own stamp box.
For teachers there is a one-day field trip, with the Broadway walk, the Local History Branch and the photo spots, and two worksheets: rephotographing an old postcard, and reading an old record.
And the recipes of the valley kitchen are now a little book to print and keep in the drawer.
